<reason>CON (Side A) built the sharper path: the motion requires employee status plus a functioning bargaining unit, and A showed the state public-sector patchwork makes that available only in some places. PRO's own answer to the pressure question (the Big Ten) conceded partiality, and A converted that into two damaging weighing moves—the antitrust shield is "a wash for half the country," and PRO's plan gives Texas/Alabama athletes the tax-and-visa cascade with no table. A also directly rebutted PRO's central premise that "the money settles employment" with the licensing-vs-employee distinction (graduate fellows, current NIL structure), which PRO never squarely answered beyond "a court might rule otherwise." A's late turn that wrestlers aren't employees under PRO's logic, so a department-wide unit collapses, went unanswered in PRO's closing. PRO's best material—the settlement class has no ratification vote and no shield, "they want the union's product without its process"—was real and well-framed, but A had answers (notice/objection rights, class counsel fiduciary duty, uniform coverage across all states). A's two clipped rebuttals were an execution cost, but the substance landed. Clear but competitive win for A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answering PRO's Big Ten example: "Grant it. One conference... the SEC produces zero," paired with the argument that the antitrust shield covers only unionized schools and therefore cannot be PRO's tiebreaker, plus the turn that non-revenue athletes aren't employees and so can't be in PRO's promised unit.</best_rebuttal>
